chapter: Technique, New Orleans influence and the school's future
title: Half-valving, bending notes and the blues scale
summary: They discuss half-valve effects, Lee Collins's records, and hitting notes above or below for the blues sound.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: What about half-valving though? That isn't legitimate. How some of them do that?

Oh no. He was talking just about the way he was holding it. Yeah. Well this... You see now a valve instrument, a trombone player, he can do all sorts of little things. Lissandos because he's got a slime and a valve instrument doesn't. And these are where the real subtlies involved in the music. And I think it would take a young guy playing. I work on that half-valve stuff all the time because I think that's where you can get the real shadings and the meanings and the blues. Anything can play. Lee Collins... I think Lee Collins playing with the Astoria Hot 8 on that Label X. And those are available in quite a few other 45s and things. It's some of the best examples on record of using your valves for different sounds. Half-valves and stuff. It really comes through. Every little thing... When he ends a phrase, he can end it on a half-valve or he bends it. Louie did a lot more of that than he used in the past and he does now.
I noticed the D does a lot of that with his lip too, not just with his... Yeah.

It's a combination of lip and valves on that. You bend notes. As a matter of fact, I never thought when I'm trying to play that I should hit it right on a button. You know? Hit it above or below to get that bending quality. That gives you the blues sound. A Negro scale has been graphically illustrated as flatting the 3rd and the 7th. You know? But actually it's every note. A Negro scale is so completely African in nature that it hasn't any relationship to a diatonic scale. At first, here it says that's what gives the music so much rough quality to it. You say rough, you can't figure it out. You say, well it has a rough sound but yet they're not playing ragged. You know? When I say ragged, I mean when they hit, hit, start off, well not starting off the tune. Because they do start off tunes kind of raggedy now and then. But when they got it down where I saw a guy who go one, two, and then they whap, they hit it. They all hit it together. But it's the rough quality of the horns. And that rough quality is hitting a note above or below to get that blues sound.
